summary: Amoxapine is a dibenzoxazepine tricyclic antidepressant (a metabolite of the antipsychotic loxapine) that inhibits norepinephrine and serotonin reuptake and also blocks dopamine receptors, giving it antidepressant plus mild antipsychotic activity. It is used for depression with anxiety, agitation or psychotic features and has a relatively rapid onset. It carries a boxed warning for suicidality in young patients and, uniquely among TCAs, can cause extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome; overdose tends to cause seizures and renal failure rather than the cardiotoxicity typical of other TCAs.
indications: Relief of symptoms of depression in neurotic or reactive depressive disorders
Depression accompanied by anxiety or agitation

moa: Amoxapine is a tricyclic dibenzoxazepine antidepressant that reduces neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, increasing their synaptic availability. It is also a dopamine (D2) receptor antagonist (a property shared with its parent antipsychotic loxapine), which contributes to mild antipsychotic activity and to extrapyramidal side effects. It is not a monoamine oxidase inhibitor.

absolute: Concomitant use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (hyperpyretic crises, severe convulsions, death)
Acute recovery phase following myocardial infarction
relative: History of seizures or conditions lowering seizure threshold
Urinary retention, narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy
Patients at risk of suicide; bipolar disorder (manic switch)

preg: Animal studies showed embryotoxicity and fetotoxicity at multiples of the human dose; there are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Amoxapine is excreted in human milk. Because effects on the infant are unknown, exercise caution when administering to a nursing woman and consider the importance of the drug to the mother.
renal: The kidney is the main route of excretion of amoxapine and its metabolites; use lower doses and cautious titration in renal impairment. Renal failure (acute tubular necrosis with rhabdomyolysis) can also complicate overdose.
hepatic: Amoxapine is almost completely metabolized in the liver; impaired hepatic function may increase plasma levels. Use lower doses with caution and monitor for toxicity; rare hepatitis has been reported.

major: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - contraindicated; risk of hyperpyretic crisis, seizures and death (allow 14-day washout)
Other serotonergic drugs - risk of serotonin syndrome
Class I antiarrhythmics / QT-prolonging drugs - additive cardiac toxicity
moderate: Anticholinergic drugs - additive effects including paralytic ileus and hyperthermia
CNS depressants / alcohol / barbiturates - enhanced sedation and respiratory depression
CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g. fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine) - markedly increased TCA levels
minor: Antihypertensives (e.g. guanethidine, clonidine) - amoxapine may blunt their effect
Thyroid agents - possible enhanced antidepressant effect and arrhythmia
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to food.
interactions.alcohol: Amoxapine enhances the response to alcohol; avoid alcohol due to additive CNS depression.
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate serum prolactin and alter EEG patterns; tricyclics can affect ECG (QRS/QT).

emergency: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)

monitoring: Mood, suicidal ideation and behavioral changes, especially early and after dose changes
Extrapyramidal signs and tardive dyskinesia on chronic use
Baseline and periodic ECG and blood pressure (orthostatic)
Signs of anticholinergic toxicity and urinary retention
Hepatic and renal function and CBC if symptoms suggest toxicity
counsel: Watch for and report worsening mood, agitation, or thoughts of self-harm, especially when starting or changing dose
Do not drink alcohol and avoid driving until you know how it affects you (drowsiness)
Report involuntary movements of face/tongue, muscle stiffness, high fever or difficulty urinating
Do not stop suddenly - taper under medical guidance to avoid withdrawal
Rise slowly from lying/sitting to limit dizziness; full effect may take a few weeks
pk: Initial clinical effect in 4-7 days; response within 2 weeks in over 80% of responders
Peak blood levels about 90 minutes after ingestion
Antidepressant effect maintained with daily dosing
Store at 20-25 C in a tight, child-resistant container
pearls: Boxed warning: antidepressants increase risk of suicidal thinking/behavior in children, adolescents and young adults (<=24 years) - monitor closely early in treatment
Unlike other TCAs, amoxapine has dopamine-blocking (loxapine-derived) activity and can cause extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Amoxapine overdose characteristically causes seizures (status epilepticus) and delayed renal failure rather than the cardiotoxicity seen with other TCAs
Onset of antidepressant effect is faster than amitriptyline or imipramine, often within the first week
Never combine with an MAOI; allow a 14-day washout when switching
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not double up. If on a single bedtime dose and the morning has passed, contact your prescriber rather than taking it during the day.
overdose: Amoxapine overdose differs from other tricyclics: serious cardiovascular effects are uncommon, but CNS toxicity predominates with frequent grand mal seizures that may progress to status epilepticus, coma and acidosis; acute renal failure (acute tubular necrosis with rhabdomyolysis/myoglobinuria) can develop 2-5 days later, mainly after multiple seizures, and fatal overdoses have occurred. Treatment is symptomatic and supportive with priority on preventing/controlling seizures (benzodiazepines), airway protection, gastric lavage and activated charcoal if early, and monitoring renal function; dialysis is not effective.
